name: Jōmon culture
evidenceNote: The Jōmon people had no writing; their long history is dated by radiocarbon and by changing styles of cord-marked pottery.
summary: The Jōmon were hunter-gatherers of the Japanese archipelago who made some of the world's earliest pottery, decorated by pressing cords into the clay ('jōmon' means 'cord-marked'). Over thousands of years many lived in settled villages such as Sannai-Maruyama, made lacquerware, clay figurines and stone circles, and managed plants. From about 900 BCE rice farmers of the Yayoi culture spread from Kyushu, and the Jōmon way of life gave way, lasting longest in the north.

name: Hoabinhian
evidenceNote: These hunter-gatherers left no writing; their sites are dated by radiocarbon on charcoal and shells in caves and rock shelters.
summary: The Hoabinhian is a stone-tool tradition of hunter-gatherers across mainland Southeast Asia, named after Hòa Bình province in Vietnam. Its typical tools are river pebbles and cobbles flaked mostly on one side. People lived in caves and rock shelters, hunting, fishing and gathering forest plants and shellfish. The tradition began in the late Ice Age and lasted into the Holocene, until farming communities with pottery and polished stone spread through the region.

name: Shangshan culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; more than 20 sites are dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The Shangshan culture of the lower Yangtze, mainly in Zhejiang, is one of the earliest settled cultures of the Holocene in China. Its people lived in villages with houses and pits, made pottery tempered with rice husks, and used a broad range of foods: rice, acorns, tubers, water chestnuts, deer, boar and fish. Residues show early use of rice, including for fermented drinks, a step on the long road to rice farming.

name: Jeulmun (Chulmun) culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; settlements and shell middens are dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Jeulmun is Korea's Neolithic, named after its comb-pattern pottery. People lived in pit-houses at sites such as Amsa-dong near Seoul, fished, hunted, gathered shellfish along the coasts and practised small-scale cultivation of plants, including foxtail millet. Large shell middens at places like Dongsam-dong record their seafood diet. The whale-hunting carvings at Bangudae are usually linked to this period. It was followed by the farming Mumun culture.

name: Pengtoushan culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, with wide variation between samples.
summary: The Pengtoushan culture of northwestern Hunan, in the middle Yangtze basin, has some of the earliest evidence of domesticated rice in China, with larger-than-wild grains dated to about 8200–7800 BCE at its type site. Its people made cord-marked pottery. The later site of Bashidang had a wall and ditch and large amounts of rice. It lived at the same time as the Peiligang culture to the north.

name: Peiligang culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; signs scratched on shells at Jiahu are debated, but most scholars do not count them as writing.
summary: The Peiligang culture of central Henan, around the Yi-Luo valley and beyond, includes more than 100 sites. Its people farmed millet, raised pigs, hunted and fished, and made some of the oldest pottery in northern China. Villages had separate cemeteries, and graves show few differences in wealth. Its best-known site, Jiahu, produced bone flutes and signs on tortoise shells.

name: Hemudu culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; waterlogged villages are dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The Hemudu culture flourished south of Hangzhou Bay in Zhejiang and on the Zhoushan islands. Its people grew rice in wet fields with bone spades, lived in long wooden houses on stilts, and made black pottery and some of the earliest lacquered wood. Waterlogged sites such as Hemudu and Tianluoshan preserved wood, seeds and bone in remarkable detail. Some scholars link it to the ancestors of Austronesian-speaking peoples.

name: Yangshao culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; signs painted on pots are not considered writing, and villages are dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The Yangshao culture of the middle Yellow River, named after a village in western Henan excavated in 1921, was a culture of millet farmers in Henan, Shaanxi and Shanxi. It is famous for painted red pottery and for planned villages such as Banpo and Jiangzhai in the Wei River valley, with houses arranged around open spaces and ditches round the edge. Later phases show growing populations and larger centres.

name: Hongshan culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; sites from Inner Mongolia to Liaoning are dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The Hongshan culture of northeast China, in western Liaoning and southeastern Inner Mongolia, is known for its carved jades, including some of the earliest jade 'pig-dragons', and for the ritual complex at Niuheliang with its 'Goddess Temple', altars and stone cairn tombs. Elite burials with jades show a ranked society with shared religious beliefs.

name: Dawenkou culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; a few signs carved on pots may be related to later scripts, but they are not writing, and sites are dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The Dawenkou culture lived mainly in Shandong, with sites in Anhui, Henan and Jiangsu, at the same time as Yangshao to the west. Graves grew increasingly unequal, some filled with jade, turquoise and ivory, and the earliest alligator-skin drums. Signs carved on some large jars are sometimes compared with later Chinese characters. Dawenkou developed into the Shandong Longshan culture.

name: Dapenkeng culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; coastal sites in Taiwan are dated by radiocarbon, and their link to Austronesian languages is a strong but indirect inference.
summary: The Dapenkeng culture is the earliest Neolithic culture of Taiwan, known from coastal sites with cord-marked pottery jars and bowls. Many archaeologists think its people crossed the Taiwan Strait from the mainland and were the ancestors of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples, speaking early Austronesian languages. If so, their descendants were part of the great Austronesian expansion that later carried related languages across Island Southeast Asia and the Pacific.

name: Liangzhu culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, and symbols carved on some objects have not been shown to be writing.
summary: The Liangzhu culture of the Yangtze delta, around Lake Tai, was the last and greatest Neolithic jade culture of China. Its rice farmers built a walled centre near Hangzhou with large dams for water control. Jade, silk, ivory and lacquer appear only in elite graves, showing a sharply ranked society that many scholars regard as an early state. It may have declined after severe flooding.

name: Majiayao culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; villages and cemeteries are dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The Majiayao culture of the upper Yellow River, in Gansu and eastern Qinghai, was a culture of farming villages famous for its painted pottery, decorated with swirling black designs and sometimes human figures, often seen as a high point of Neolithic Chinese pottery. It developed from Yangshao traditions on the western edge of the farming world of northern China.

name: Longshan culture
evidenceNote: No writing has been found; towns such as Taosi and Shimao are dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The Longshan culture of the middle and lower Yellow River is named after a site in Shandong and is known for thin, highly polished black 'eggshell' pottery made on the wheel. Populations grew sharply in the third millennium BCE, and many towns had rammed-earth walls; regional variants in Henan, Shanxi and Shaanxi include great centres such as Taosi and Shimao. It led into the Erlitou culture.

name: Ban Chiang culture
dateLabel: c. 2000 or 1500 BCE – c. 200 CE (start disputed)
evidenceNote: No writing existed, and archaeologists disagree by up to 1,000 years about when farming villages and bronze began here.
summary: The Ban Chiang tradition of the Khorat Plateau in northeast Thailand is known from village cemeteries with red-painted pottery, bronze and later iron. Its people grew rice and kept domestic animals. Its dating is a famous debate: early claims of bronze before 3000 BCE were rejected, but scholars still disagree whether settlement began around 2000 or 1500 BCE and bronze around 2000 or 1000 BCE.

name: Erlitou culture
evidenceNote: Erlitou is well dated by radiocarbon, but without writing no one can prove whether it was the Xia dynasty of later histories.
summary: The Erlitou culture of western Henan and southern Shanxi was an early Bronze Age society, seen by most archaeologists as China's first state. Its capital near Yanshi had palaces, roads and bronze foundries that made the first ritual bronze vessels. Many Chinese scholars identify it with the late Xia dynasty of traditional histories; others call this premature, since no Xia writing has been found. It was followed by the Erligang (early Shang) culture.

name: Sanxingdui culture
evidenceNote: No readable writing has been found; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, and its link to the later kingdom of Shu comes from later texts.
summary: The Sanxingdui culture of the Chengdu Plain in Sichuan built a walled city at Sanxingdui and cast extraordinary bronzes, including large heads and masks with bulging eyes and gold-foil faces, quite unlike those of the Shang. It grew out of the earlier Baodun culture and was followed by the Jinsha phase. Many archaeologists link it to the ancient kingdom of Shu.

name: Lapita culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; sites are dated by radiocarbon and, at Nukuleka in Tonga, by precise uranium-thorium dates on coral tools.
summary: The Lapita people were the first to settle the remote Pacific. Known from finely stamped pottery, they appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1600–1200 BCE, then within a few centuries sailed to the Solomons, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, islands no one had reached before. Their descendants became the Polynesians. More than 200 Lapita sites are known.

sources.title: Burley, Weisler & Zhao (2012), High Precision U/Th Dating of First Polynesian Settlement, PLoS ONE 7(11)

name: Mumun culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed in Korea yet; villages and dolmens are dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.
summary: The Mumun ('plain pottery') culture of Korea followed the Jeulmun and brought intensive farming of rice and millet, large villages of pit-houses, and growing differences in rank. Its people built most of Korea's dolmens, and some villages, such as Songguk-ri, had palisades and ditches. Local bronze-working is not proven before about the 13th century BCE and bronze stayed rare until after 300 BCE.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites

name: Đông Sơn culture
evidenceNote: The Đông Sơn people left no writing of their own; the culture is known from excavation, and Chinese texts describe the region only from outside.
summary: The Đông Sơn culture, centred on the Red River delta and nearby valleys of northern Vietnam, was a Bronze Age society of rice farmers, fishers and sailors, often linked with the Lạc Việt. It is famous for large bronze drums cast with scenes of boats, warriors and houses, found widely across northern Vietnam, Yunnan and Guangxi, and as far as Malaysia. The fortified city of Cổ Loa belongs to its later phase.

name: Sa Huỳnh culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the culture is known from jar-burial cemeteries dated by radiocarbon and imported objects.
summary: The Sa Huỳnh culture of central and southern Vietnam is known from cemeteries of burial jars rich in locally made iron tools and weapons, glass beads and ornaments of jade and glass, and shows evidence of a wide trade network across the South China Sea. Its first site was found in 1909. The Sa Huỳnh people were most likely ancestors of the Austronesian-speaking Cham, who later founded the kingdom of Champa.

name: Yayoi culture
dateLabel: c. 900 BCE – 250 CE (start debated; older view c. 300 BCE)
evidenceNote: The Yayoi wrote nothing themselves; the start date comes from debated radiocarbon results, though Chinese histories describe the land of Wa from the 1st century CE.
summary: The Yayoi culture brought wet-rice farming, bronze and iron to Japan, spreading from northern Kyushu after migrants arrived from the Korean Peninsula. Radiocarbon dating has pushed its start back from about 300 BCE to the 10th–8th centuries BCE, though this is still debated. Villages such as Yoshinogari grew into fortified centres, and Chinese histories describe the many chiefdoms of 'Wa' and the queen Himiko.

name: Kofun culture (early Yamato)
evidenceNote: Chinese histories such as the Book of Song mention the kings of Wa, but Japan's own chronicles were written only in the 8th century.
summary: The Kofun period is named after the great keyhole-shaped burial mounds built for Japan's rulers from the mid-3rd century, such as Hashihaka and Daisenryō. They mark the rise of the Yamato kingship in the Kinai region, which came to dominate much of Japan. Chinese histories record Yamato's contacts with China from the late 4th century, and Buddhism and Chinese writing came from Baekje in Korea near the end of the period.
